words.def: Able to recover quickly from difficult conditions or setbacks.
words.simple: Able to get better fast after something bad happens.
words.easy: Kids are more [resilient] than we think.
ex: The economy proved surprisingly [resilient] during the crisis.
She's a [resilient] person who never stays down for long.
Building a [resilient] team takes time and trust.
words.nuance: Resilient is about bouncing back after a blow. Tough is about not breaking in the first place; robust describes strong, well-built systems and things.
words.ety: Latin resilire 'to leap back'.

prec.s: After losing her job and her home in the same year, she bounced back quickly — she's remarkably ___.
prec.why: Resilient means recovering quickly after hardship — 'bounced back'. Robust suits strong systems and objects; rigid means unable to bend; stubborn means refusing to change your mind.

words.def: Logical and consistent, forming a clear whole; (of a person) able to speak clearly.
words.simple: Clear and easy to follow, with parts that fit together.
words.easy: He was too tired to give a [coherent] answer.
ex: The party still lacks a [coherent] plan for the economy.
Her essay is well researched and [coherent].
After the accident, he wasn't fully [coherent] for an hour.
words.nuance: Coherent means the parts hang together logically. Lucid stresses clarity of expression; consistent means not contradicting itself over time.
words.ety: Latin cohaerere 'to stick together'.

prec.s: The government has announced dozens of measures but still has no ___ plan that ties them together.
prec.why: Coherent means logically connected into a clear whole. Cohesive describes groups that stick together (a cohesive team); an adherent is a follower; concise means short.

words.def: Open to more than one interpretation; not having one obvious meaning.
words.simple: Able to be understood in more than one way.
words.easy: His message was [ambiguous], so I called him.
ex: The contract is [ambiguous] about who pays for repairs.
The ending of the film is deliberately [ambiguous].
Avoid [ambiguous] words in instructions.
words.nuance: Ambiguous means it could mean two (or more) specific things. Vague means not detailed or exact; equivocal suggests deliberate vagueness to avoid commitment.
words.ety: Latin ambiguus 'doubtful', from ambigere 'to wander about'.

prec.s: "I saw her duck" is ___: it could mean her bird or her quick movement.
prec.why: Ambiguous means having two possible meanings, exactly like this sentence. Ambivalent describes mixed feelings; vague means not detailed; obscure means little known or hard to understand.

words.def: Possible to do easily or conveniently; practicable.
words.simple: Possible to do in real life.
words.easy: Is it [feasible] to finish by Friday?
ex: Building a bridge here isn't technically [feasible].
We need a [feasible] plan, not a dream.
The study will look at the [feasibility] of a new railway.
words.nuance: Feasible asks 'can it be done?'. Viable asks 'will it work and survive?', often about money; plausible asks 'is it believable?'.
words.ety: Old French faisible, from faire 'to do', Latin facere.

prec.s: With only two engineers, it isn't ___ to launch the app in all twenty countries this month.
prec.why: Feasible means possible to actually do. Plausible means believable; probable means likely to happen; eligible means meeting the conditions for something.

words.def: Seeming reasonable or probable; believable.
words.simple: Seeming likely to be true.
words.easy: That's a [plausible] excuse, but I don't believe it.
ex: Scientists offered a [plausible] explanation for the strange lights.
It's [plausible] that the email was sent by mistake.
His story sounded [plausible] at first.
words.nuance: Plausible means it seems true, without proving it — sometimes with a hint of doubt. Credible means worthy of belief, often about people or sources.
words.ety: Latin plausibilis 'deserving applause', from plaudere 'to clap'.

prec.s: Nobody knows why the ship sank, but the most ___ theory is that it hit a rock.
prec.why: Plausible means likely to be true — right for theories and explanations. Feasible and viable are about whether a plan can work; palpable means so strong you can almost touch it.

words.def: Widespread in a particular area or at a particular time.
words.simple: Common in a place or among a group of people.
words.easy: Back pain is [prevalent] among office workers.
ex: The disease is more [prevalent] in warm climates.
These attitudes were [prevalent] in the 1950s.
Researchers measured the [prevalence] of smoking among teenagers.
words.nuance: Prevalent is neutral and often statistical (prevalence of a disease). Rife is for bad things; pervasive stresses spreading through everything.
words.ety: Latin praevalere 'to be very strong'.

prec.s: Short-sightedness is far more ___ among children who spend little time outdoors.
prec.why: Prevalent means common among a group — the standard word for how often a condition occurs. Prominent means easy to see or famous; predominant means the strongest or largest; relevant means connected.

words.def: Very great or intense; showing deep insight.
words.simple: Very deep or very strong.
words.easy: The trip had a [profound] effect on me.
ex: The internet has brought [profound] changes to how we work.
She said something simple but [profound].
He was [profoundly] grateful for their help.
words.nuance: Profound is about depth — of effects, feelings or thoughts. Significant means important; dramatic means sudden and striking.
words.ety: Latin profundus 'deep', from fundus 'bottom'.

prec.s: Losing his father at twelve had a ___ effect on the rest of his life.
prec.why: A profound effect is deep and lasting. Profuse means flowing in large amounts (profuse apologies); prolific means producing a lot; pompous means self-important.

words.def: Strong and healthy; sturdily built; (of a system or argument) able to withstand problems.
words.simple: Strong and hard to break.
words.easy: We need a [robust] plan that works in any weather.
ex: The new software is fast and [robust].
Despite her age, she's in [robust] health.
The minister gave a [robust] defence of the policy.
words.nuance: Robust suits systems, evidence and bodies that hold up under pressure. Resilient is about recovering after a blow; sturdy is about physical solidity.
words.ety: Latin robustus 'firm and hard', from robur 'oak'.

prec.s: The bank needs a ___ computer system that won't crash when millions of people log in at once.
prec.why: Robust describes systems strong enough not to fail under pressure. Resilient is recovering after failure; rigorous means thorough and strict; rugged means rough and tough, like terrain or outdoor gear.

words.def: Perceptible by touch; clear and definite; real.
words.simple: Real, so you can see or touch it.
words.easy: We need [tangible] results, not more talk.
ex: The new policy has had no [tangible] benefits so far.
There was a [tangible] sense of relief in the room.
Trust is valuable, even though it's [intangible].
words.nuance: Tangible means real and measurable — benefits, results, evidence. Palpable is used for feelings so strong you can almost touch them.
words.ety: Latin tangere 'to touch'.

prec.s: After six months of meetings, the project still hasn't produced any ___ results.
prec.why: Tangible results are real and measurable. Palpable suits feelings (palpable tension); potential means possible in the future; tentative means not certain or final.

words.def: Exposed to the possibility of being attacked or harmed, physically or emotionally.
words.simple: Easy to hurt or harm.
words.easy: Old people are more [vulnerable] in very hot weather.
ex: Children are especially [vulnerable] to online scams.
He felt [vulnerable] after sharing his story.
The attack showed how [vulnerable] the network was.
words.nuance: Vulnerable means open to harm, physically or emotionally — and, in modern use, willing to show feelings. Susceptible means likely to be affected by something specific (an illness, flattery).
words.ety: Late Latin vulnerabilis, from vulnus 'wound'.

prec.s: Without a password, your account is ___ to anyone who finds your phone.
prec.why: Vulnerable to = open to harm from. Venerable means respected because of age; volatile means changing suddenly; valuable means worth a lot.

words.def: Able to adapt or be adapted to many different functions or activities.
words.simple: Able to do many different things well.
words.easy: Eggs are a [versatile] food.
ex: She's a [versatile] actor who can play any role.
This jacket is [versatile] enough for work and weekends.
Python is a [versatile] programming language.
words.nuance: Versatile praises a person or thing with many uses or skills. Flexible means able to change plans easily; adaptable means able to adjust to new situations.
words.ety: Latin versatilis 'turning easily', from vertere 'to turn'.

prec.s: A ___ player, he can defend, attack or play in goal if needed.
prec.why: Versatile means skilled in many roles. Volatile means changing suddenly; verbose means using too many words; vertical means upright.

words.def: Very complicated or detailed.
words.simple: Having many small parts or details.
words.easy: She makes [intricate] paper designs by hand.
ex: The carpet has an [intricate] pattern of flowers.
The novel's plot is [intricate] but rewarding.
He explained the [intricacies] of the tax system.
words.nuance: Intricate stresses many small, finely connected details — often admired. Complicated is often negative; elaborate means carefully planned with lots of parts.
words.ety: Latin intricare 'to entangle'.

prec.s: The watchmaker spent weeks on the ___ mechanism, with over 300 tiny parts.
prec.why: Intricate means made of many small detailed parts. Intimate means close and personal; integral means essential to a whole; intrinsic means part of something's basic nature.

words.def: No longer produced or used; out of date.
words.simple: No longer used, because something newer exists.
words.easy: My old phone is now [obsolete].
ex: Typewriters became [obsolete] in the 1990s.
New technology could make many jobs [obsolete].
The law is [obsolete] and should be changed.
words.nuance: Obsolete means replaced and no longer used. Old-fashioned means no longer in style; an anachronism belongs to a different time.
words.ety: Latin obsoletus 'grown old, worn out'.

prec.s: Once digital cameras arrived, film cameras became almost ___ for most people.
prec.why: Obsolete means no longer used because something better replaced it. Absolute means complete; obscure means little known; obstinate means stubborn.

words.def: Refusing to be persuaded or to change one's mind.
words.simple: Very sure and not willing to change your mind.
words.easy: She was [adamant] that she had locked the door.
ex: He's [adamant] that he didn't take the money.
The coach was [adamant] about the new rules.
They [adamantly] refused to sign.
words.nuance: Adamant is about firmly insisting on something you say or believe — often neutral. Obstinate is critical: stubborn without good reason.
words.ety: Greek adamas 'untameable, very hard stone'.

prec.s: Despite the evidence, the witness was ___ that she had seen the driver's face.
prec.why: Adamant means insisting firmly. Ambivalent means having mixed feelings; apathetic means not caring; amenable means open to persuasion — the opposite.

words.def: (adj.) Able to express ideas clearly; (v., /ɑːrˈtɪkjəleɪt/) to express an idea clearly in words.
words.simple: Good at saying clearly what you think.
words.easy: She's smart and very [articulate].
ex: He's an [articulate] speaker who explains complex ideas simply.
She struggled to [articulate] how she felt.
The report clearly [articulates] the problems.
words.nuance: Articulate stresses clarity; eloquent adds beauty and emotional power. Fluent is about speaking smoothly, especially in a language.
words.ety: Latin articulare 'to divide into joints, speak distinctly'.

prec.s: Many children know they feel sad but can't ___ why.
prec.why: Articulate (verb) means put a thought or feeling clearly into words. Accentuate means emphasise; allocate means share out; accumulate means gather over time.

words.def: To become progressively worse.
words.simple: To slowly get worse.
words.easy: His health began to [deteriorate] last year.
ex: Relations between the two countries have [deteriorated].
The weather [deteriorated] as we climbed.
Without care, old buildings [deteriorate] quickly.
words.nuance: Deteriorate means get worse over time, by itself. Exacerbate means make a problem worse (it needs an object); decline is more neutral.
words.ety: Late Latin deteriorare, from deterior 'worse'.

prec.s: Without regular repairs, the old bridge will continue to ___.
prec.why: Deteriorate means get worse by itself — no object needed. Exacerbate and aggravate need an object (make something worse); decimate means destroy a large part of.

words.def: A lack of compatibility or similarity between two or more facts.
words.simple: A difference between two things that should be the same.
words.easy: There's a [discrepancy] between the bill and the price on the menu.
ex: Auditors found a [discrepancy] of $5,000 in the accounts.
There are [discrepancies] between the two witness reports.
We need to explain the [discrepancy] in the data.
words.nuance: A discrepancy is a mismatch between things that should agree — figures, accounts, records. A disparity is an unfair difference (between rich and poor).
words.ety: Latin discrepare 'to sound differently'.

prec.s: The accountant noticed a small ___ between the bank statement and the company's records.
prec.why: A discrepancy is a mismatch between records that should agree. A disparity is an unfair gap (wage disparity); a dichotomy is a split into two opposites; a disposition is a person's nature.

words.def: Difficult to find, catch, achieve, define or remember.
words.simple: Hard to find, catch or achieve.
words.easy: For years, success remained [elusive].
ex: The [elusive] leopard is rarely seen in the wild.
A cure for the common cold remains [elusive].
Happiness can be [elusive] if you chase it too hard.
words.nuance: Elusive describes something hard to catch or achieve. Evasive describes a person deliberately avoiding questions.
words.ety: Latin eludere 'to escape by trickery', from ludere 'to play'.

prec.s: Despite decades of research, a cure for the disease remains ___.
prec.why: Elusive means hard to achieve or find. Evasive describes people dodging questions; illusory means not real; allusive means full of indirect references.

words.def: Stated clearly and in detail, leaving no room for doubt; showing sex or violence openly.
words.simple: Said clearly and directly, so nothing is hidden.
words.easy: The rules are [explicit]: no phones in class.
ex: She gave [explicit] instructions not to open the box.
The law makes [explicit] reference to online abuse.
The film contains [explicit] scenes.
words.nuance: Explicit is the opposite of implicit: stated openly rather than suggested. It can also mean showing sexual content openly.
words.ety: Latin explicitus 'unfolded', from plicare 'to fold'.

prec.s: The manager didn't just hint; she gave ___ instructions: 'Nobody leaves before six.'
prec.why: Explicit means stated clearly and directly. Implicit and tacit mean understood without being said — the opposite; elaborate means detailed and complex.

words.def: Suggested though not directly expressed; (of trust) complete and unquestioning.
words.simple: Understood without being said directly.
words.easy: There was an [implicit] threat in his voice.
ex: Her silence was an [implicit] criticism of the plan.
I trust her [implicitly].
Studies show we all have [implicit] biases.
words.nuance: Implicit means contained in what is said without being stated. Tacit is specifically about unspoken agreement or approval. 'Trust implicitly' means trust completely.
words.ety: Latin implicitus 'entangled', from plicare 'to fold'.

prec.s: Although no one said it, there was an ___ message in the email: work harder or leave.
prec.why: Implicit means suggested without being said. Explicit is the opposite; imminent means about to happen; illicit means illegal.

words.def: To make someone feel isolated or estranged; to cause someone to stop supporting you.
words.simple: To make people stop liking or supporting you.
words.easy: His rude jokes [alienated] his friends.
ex: The new prices could [alienate] loyal customers.
Many young people feel [alienated] from politics.
She didn't want to [alienate] her colleagues by complaining.
words.nuance: Alienate means push people away so they no longer feel part of something. Antagonize means make someone hostile; ostracize means a group deliberately excludes someone.
words.ety: Latin alienare 'to make another's', from alienus 'of another'.

prec.s: The party's extreme new policies risk ___ the moderate voters it needs to win.
prec.why: Alienate means push people away so they stop supporting you. Ostracize is a group shutting someone out; eliminate means remove; alleviate means ease pain.

words.def: To support or strengthen; to prop up.
words.simple: To make something stronger or more certain.
words.easy: The win [bolstered] the team's confidence.
ex: The new data [bolster] the case for change.
The government cut taxes to [bolster] the economy.
Good reviews [bolstered] sales.
words.nuance: Bolster means add strength or support to something that may be weak. Boost is more informal; reinforce suggests adding extra strength.
words.ety: Old English bolster 'a long pillow' — something to prop you up.

prec.s: Winning the first three games has ___ the young team's confidence.
prec.why: Bolster means strengthen. Bloat means swell up; boast means brag; bombard means attack continuously.

words.def: To reduce in extent or quantity; to impose a restriction on.
words.simple: To cut or limit something.
words.easy: Bad weather [curtailed] our trip.
ex: The new law [curtails] the power of the police.
Spending was [curtailed] after the crisis.
Her career was [curtailed] by injury.
words.nuance: Curtail means cut short or limit, often by authority or circumstances. Reduce is neutral; restrict stresses rules that limit.
words.ety: From obsolete curtal 'horse with a docked tail', influenced by tail.

prec.s: The government plans to ___ the use of plastic bags with a new tax.
prec.why: Curtail means cut back or limit. Curate means select and organise; corroborate means confirm; cultivate means grow or develop.

words.def: To use up the supply or resources of something.
words.simple: To use up most of something.
words.easy: The long trip [depleted] our savings.
ex: Overfishing has [depleted] stocks of cod.
Stress can [deplete] your energy.
The ozone layer was [depleted] by chemicals.
words.nuance: Deplete means reduce a supply until little is left. Exhaust means use up completely; drain suggests a steady loss.
words.ety: Latin deplere 'to empty out'.

prec.s: Years of drought have ___ the region's water supply.
prec.why: Deplete means use up a supply. Deplore means strongly disapprove of; deport means send out of a country; deprive needs a person and 'of' (deprived people of water).

words.def: To destroy completely; to put an end to.
words.simple: To remove something completely.
words.easy: The goal is to [eradicate] the disease.
ex: Smallpox was [eradicated] in 1980.
The charity aims to [eradicate] child hunger.
Corruption is hard to [eradicate].
words.nuance: Eradicate means remove completely, down to the roots — diseases, poverty, pests. Eliminate is more general; abolish is used for laws and systems.
words.ety: Latin eradicare 'to tear out by the roots', from radix 'root'.

prec.s: Thanks to vaccines, polio has been almost completely ___ worldwide.
prec.why: Eradicate is the standard verb for wiping out a disease. Abolish is for laws and systems; evacuate means move people out of danger; exempt means free from a rule.

words.def: To encourage the development of something; to bring up a child that is not one's own.
words.simple: To help something grow or develop.
words.easy: Good teachers [foster] a love of reading.
ex: The program aims to [foster] cooperation between schools.
Open offices are meant to [foster] creativity.
They [fostered] three children over ten years.
words.nuance: Foster means create the conditions for something to develop (a feeling, relationship, idea). Nurture adds care and protection; promote is more active publicity.
words.ety: Old English fōstrian 'to feed, nourish'.

prec.s: The new manager organised team lunches to ___ a sense of community.
prec.why: Foster means help a feeling or relationship grow. Fester means get worse (a wound or anger); forge ahead means move forward quickly; falter means lose strength.

words.def: To hinder or impede the movement or progress of.
words.simple: To make it harder for something to happen or move.
words.easy: Heavy rain [hampered] the search.
ex: A lack of money has [hampered] the project.
The team was [hampered] by injuries all season.
Strict rules [hamper] small businesses.
words.nuance: Hamper means get in the way and slow progress. Impede is more formal; obstruct suggests blocking completely or deliberately.
words.ety: Possibly from Old Norse hemja 'to restrain'.

prec.s: Rescue efforts were ___ by strong winds and heavy snow.
prec.why: Hamper means make progress harder. Hammer means hit hard; pamper means treat with too much care; tamper (with) means interfere illegally.

words.def: To weaken something gradually or secretly; to damage confidence or authority.
words.simple: To slowly make someone or something weaker.
words.easy: Don't [undermine] your teacher in front of the class.
ex: The scandal [undermined] trust in the government.
Constant criticism can [undermine] a child's confidence.
Fake news [undermines] democracy.
words.nuance: Undermine means weaken gradually, often from below or behind. Sabotage means deliberately destroy; subvert means overturn a system or authority.
words.ety: Originally 'to dig a mine under' a wall to make it collapse.

prec.s: Every time the manager says yes, the CEO says no — he keeps ___ her authority.
prec.why: Undermine means weaken someone's authority. Underestimate means think something is smaller than it is; underline means emphasise; undertake means take on a task.

words.def: Large or heavy and difficult to carry or use; slow and complicated.
words.simple: Big, heavy or slow, so it's hard to use.
words.easy: The old system is [cumbersome] and slow.
ex: The [cumbersome] suitcase wouldn't fit in the car.
Applying for a visa is a [cumbersome] process.
Early computers were [cumbersome] machines.
words.nuance: Cumbersome is used for heavy objects and for slow, complicated procedures. Bulky is only about size; unwieldy stresses difficulty of handling.
words.ety: From cumber 'to hinder' + -some.

prec.s: To get a refund you must fill in five forms and wait three months — a truly ___ process.
prec.why: Cumbersome means slow and complicated. Cumulative means increasing by adding up; compelling means convincing; comprehensive means complete.

words.def: Seeming difficult to deal with in anticipation; intimidating.
words.simple: Looking so hard that it makes you a little afraid.
words.easy: Starting a new job can be [daunting].
ex: Writing a book is a [daunting] task.
The size of the problem is [daunting].
She faced the [daunting] climb with a smile.
words.nuance: Daunting describes a task that looks hard before you start, making you hesitate. Overwhelming means too much to handle; formidable adds respect for the difficulty.
words.ety: Old French danter, from Latin domare 'to tame'.

prec.s: Learning a new language at fifty can seem ___, but small daily steps make it possible.
prec.why: Daunting means looking hard enough to discourage you. Doting means very loving; dormant means inactive; diligent means hard-working.

words.def: Not having any serious purpose or value; not serious.
words.simple: Silly and not important.
words.easy: Don't waste money on [frivolous] things.
ex: The court threw out the [frivolous] lawsuit.
It's not a [frivolous] question — please take it seriously.
They spent the bonus on [frivolous] luxuries.
words.nuance: Frivolous criticises something as not serious when it should be (or as a waste of money). Trivial means unimportant; light-hearted is positive — cheerful and fun.
words.ety: Latin frivolus 'silly, trifling'.

prec.s: The judge dismissed the case as ___: the man had sued a café because his coffee was too hot.
prec.why: Frivolous means not serious, without real purpose — ideal for a silly lawsuit. Fervent means passionate; furtive means secretive; fastidious means very particular.

words.def: Easily persuaded to believe something; credulous.
words.simple: Too quick to believe what people tell you.
words.easy: Don't be so [gullible] — it's a scam.
ex: [Gullible] tourists paid for fake tickets.
I was [gullible] enough to lend him money.
The ad was aimed at [gullible] buyers.
words.nuance: Gullible is the everyday word for easily tricked; credulous is its formal equivalent. Naive means lacking experience, not necessarily tricked.
words.ety: From gull 'to fool', perhaps from gull 'a young bird'.

prec.s: Only a ___ person would believe an email saying they'd won a lottery they never entered.
prec.why: Gullible means easily tricked. Genial means friendly; garrulous means very talkative; grateful means thankful.

words.def: More merciful or tolerant than expected, especially in punishment.
words.simple: Not strict when someone breaks a rule.
words.easy: My parents were [lenient] about bedtime.
ex: The judge gave him a [lenient] sentence.
Some say the new rules are too [lenient].
She asked the court for [leniency].
words.nuance: Lenient is about going easy on punishment or rules. Permissive means allowing too much freedom, often critical; tolerant means accepting differences.
words.ety: Latin lenire 'to soothe', from lenis 'mild'.

prec.s: Critics said three months was far too ___ a sentence for such a serious crime.
prec.why: Lenient means not strict in punishment. Lethal means deadly; lucid means clear; lavish means extravagant.

words.def: Too long, slow or dull; tiresome.
words.simple: Boring because it takes long and is always the same.
words.easy: Filling in forms is [tedious].
ex: The meeting was long and [tedious].
Data entry is [tedious] but necessary.
The film's second half becomes [tedious].
words.nuance: Tedious stresses boredom from length and repetition. Mundane means ordinary; monotonous means always the same tone or rhythm.
words.ety: Late Latin taediosus, from taedium 'weariness'.

prec.s: Copying 2,000 phone numbers into a spreadsheet by hand is a ___ job.
prec.why: Tedious means boring because long and repetitive. Tenacious means determined; tentative means hesitant; tenuous means weak.

words.def: Never done or known before.
words.simple: Never happened before.
words.easy: The city saw [unprecedented] snow this year.
ex: The pandemic caused [unprecedented] disruption.
Prices rose at an [unprecedented] rate.
It was an [unprecedented] decision by the court.
words.nuance: Unprecedented means nothing like it has happened before. It's overused in news; save it for genuinely new events.
words.ety: un- + precedent, from Latin praecedere 'to go before'.

prec.s: Nothing like it had ever happened: the stock market fell by an ___ 40% in one day.
prec.why: Unprecedented means never happened before. Unwarranted means not justified; unanimous means agreed by everyone; uninhibited means free of shyness.

words.def: Of little value or importance.
words.simple: Small and not important.
words.easy: They argued about something [trivial].
ex: Don't bother the boss with [trivial] questions.
The difference is [trivial].
It's not a [trivial] problem — it could cost millions.
words.nuance: Trivial means unimportant. Negligible means too small to matter in amount; petty adds small-mindedness.
words.ety: Latin trivialis 'commonplace', from trivium 'place where three roads meet'.

prec.s: The couple divorced after twenty years of arguing over ___ things like who left the lights on.
prec.why: Trivial (adjective) means unimportant. Trivia is a noun (small facts); traumatic means deeply upsetting; triumphant means victorious.

words.def: To have something as the main or basic point.
words.simple: To have one main point or reason.
words.easy: It all [boils down to] money.
ex: The problem [boils down to] poor communication.
In the end, it [boiled down to] a choice between two jobs.
What it [boils down to] is trust.
words.nuance: Boil down to reduces a complicated issue to its core, like boiling liquid until only the essence remains. Come down to is very close.
words.ety: From cooking: boiling a sauce to reduce it.

prec.s: We discussed the plan for hours, but in the end it all ___ one question: can we afford it?
prec.why: Boil down to = have as its main point. Break down means stop working or lose control of emotions; boil over means (anger) explode; back down means give up a position.

words.def: To improve a skill or knowledge that has weakened.
words.simple: To study something again so you get better at it.
words.easy: I need to [brush up on] my French before the trip.
ex: She [brushed up on] her maths before the exam.
It's worth [brushing up on] interview skills.
He's [brushing up on] his history.
words.nuance: Brush up on is for refreshing skills or knowledge you already had. Learn is from scratch; revise (UK) is studying for an exam.
words.ety: Like brushing dust off something old so it shines again.

prec.s: Before my trip to Madrid, I want to ___ the Spanish I learned at school.
prec.why: Brush up on = refresh old knowledge. Brush off and brush aside mean dismiss; touch on means mention briefly.

words.def: To become popular; to understand something.
words.simple: To become popular, or to start to understand.
words.easy: The new app never really [caught on].
ex: The trend quickly [caught on] among teenagers.
It took me a while to [catch on] to the joke.
Electric bikes have really [caught on] in cities.
words.nuance: Catch on has two meanings: become popular (a trend) and understand (catch on to a joke). Take off is used for fast success.
words.ety: Like catching something thrown — the idea is caught by many people.

prec.s: Video calls existed for decades but only really ___ during the pandemic.
prec.why: Catch on = become popular. Catch up means reach the same level; be caught out means be found making a mistake; call off means cancel.

words.def: To continue an action or task to its completion.
words.simple: To finish what you started or do what you promised.
words.easy: He makes plans but never [follows through].
ex: The government must [follow through] on its promises.
Good managers [follow through] on what they say.
She didn't [follow through] with the complaint.
words.nuance: Follow through stresses finishing what you committed to. Carry out means perform a task; see something through means stick with it until the end.
words.ety: From sport: continuing the movement after hitting a ball.

prec.s: Voters are tired of politicians who make big promises and then fail to ___.
prec.why: Follow through = finish what you promised. Fall through means (a plan) fails to happen; follow suit means do the same as others; fall back means retreat.

words.def: To communicate an idea successfully.
words.simple: To make people understand an idea.
words.easy: I tried to [get across] how important it was.
ex: The ad [gets its message across] in five seconds.
Teachers use stories to [get across] hard ideas.
I couldn't [get across] what I meant.
words.nuance: Get across focuses on success in making people understand. Convey is the formal word; come across (as) is about the impression you make.
words.ety: Like carrying an idea across a gap to the listener.

prec.s: Her presentation used simple charts to ___ a very complex idea.
prec.why: Get across = make people understand. Come across means seem or find by chance; get over means recover from; get around means avoid a rule or travel.

words.def: To stop using or providing something gradually, in stages.
words.simple: To stop using something slowly, step by step.
words.easy: The city will [phase out] old buses by 2030.
ex: The government plans to [phase out] coal power.
The old model is being [phased out].
Paper tickets were [phased out] last year.
words.nuance: Phase out means end something in planned stages. Scrap means end suddenly; wind down is for activities or businesses slowly closing.
words.ety: From phase 'a stage in a process'.

prec.s: The bank will ___ paper statements over the next two years, starting with younger customers.
prec.why: Phase out = gradually stop using. Phase in is the opposite (gradually introduce); pass out means faint; pay off means succeed or repay.

words.def: To postpone something; to make someone dislike or lose interest in something.
words.simple: To move something to a later time, or to make someone not want something.
words.easy: Stop [putting off] your homework!
ex: We had to [put off] the wedding until spring.
The smell [put me off] my food.
Don't be [put off] by the long queue — it moves fast.
words.nuance: Put off has two meanings: postpone (put off a meeting) and discourage (put someone off). Postpone is the formal word for the first.
words.ety: To put something away from the present moment.

prec.s: I've been ___ calling the dentist for months because I hate injections.
prec.why: Put off = delay doing something. Put up means build or let someone stay; put out means extinguish; put across means communicate.

words.def: An attempt or guess that is unlikely to succeed.
words.simple: Something that probably won't work, but you try anyway.
words.easy: It's [a long shot], but maybe she still has the keys.
ex: Winning the league is [a long shot] this year.
Applying to Harvard was [a long shot], but she got in.
It's [a long shot], but it's worth a try.
col: a bit of a long shot
words.nuance: A long shot is a hopeful attempt with low odds. 'Not by a long shot' means 'not at all'.
words.ety: From shooting or betting: a shot from far away rarely hits.

prec.s: Getting tickets the day before the final is ___, but let's try the box office anyway.
prec.why: A long shot is unlikely but worth trying. A foregone conclusion is certain; par for the course is normal and expected; a blessing in disguise turns out well.

words.def: Back to the starting point, with no progress made.
words.simple: Back to the start, after something failed.
words.easy: The deal fell through, so we're [back to square one].
ex: The test failed, and the scientists were [back to square one].
If the bank says no, we're [back to square one].
After the breakup, I felt [back to square one].
col: send someone back to square one
words.nuance: Back to square one stresses lost progress. Back to the drawing board stresses the need for a new plan.
words.ety: Possibly from board games, or early football radio commentary using a numbered grid.

prec.s: The buyer pulled out the day before signing, so we're ___ with the sale of the house.
prec.why: Back to square one = back at the start, all progress lost. On the same page means in agreement; in the same boat means in the same difficult situation; on the fence means undecided.

words.def: To stop working on something, for now or permanently.
words.simple: To stop working for today, or to stop doing something.
words.easy: It's late — let's [call it a day].
ex: After ten hours, the team [called it a day].
The band [called it a day] after thirty years.
I'm tired; I'm going to [call it a day].
col: decide to call it a day
words.nuance: Call it a day can mean stop for today or stop for good (a career, a relationship). 'Call it a night' is used in the evening.
words.ety: From the older 'call it half a day', meaning stop working early.

prec.s: We've been painting since eight this morning — let's ___ and finish tomorrow.
prec.why: Call it a day = stop working for now. Cut corners means do a job badly to save time; go the extra mile means make extra effort; bite the bullet means do something unpleasant.

words.def: In trouble, especially because of something you have done.
words.simple: In trouble because of something you did.
words.easy: He's [in hot water] for missing work.
ex: The company is [in hot water] over its data use.
I'll be [in hot water] if I'm late again.
The minister landed [in hot water] after his comments.
words.nuance: In hot water means in trouble with someone in authority because of your own actions.
words.ety: Hot water as a picture of an uncomfortable, dangerous situation.

prec.s: The football club is ___ after fans damaged the visitors' stadium.
prec.why: In hot water = in trouble for something done. On cloud nine means very happy; in the same boat means sharing a difficulty; out of the woods means out of danger.

words.def: The last of a series of annoyances that finally makes a situation unbearable.
words.simple: The last small problem that makes you finally get too angry to go on.
words.easy: When he was late again, it was [the last straw].
ex: The price rise was [the last straw] for many customers.
Losing the final was [the last straw] for the coach.
His rude email was [the last straw], so I quit.
col: be the last straw for someone
words.nuance: The last straw is a small event that, after many others, finally breaks your patience. Hebrew has the same image: הקש ששבר את גב הגמל.
words.ety: From the proverb 'the straw that broke the camel's back'.

prec.s: My neighbour played loud music every night for a year; the drum solo at 3 a.m. was ___.
prec.why: The last straw finally ends your patience after many problems. The tip of the iceberg is a small visible part of a big problem; the lion's share is the biggest part; a red herring is a distraction.

words.word: the ball is in your court
words.ipa: ðə ˈbɔːl ɪz ɪn jər ˈkɔːrt
words.def: It is your turn to take action or make a decision.
words.simple: Now it's your turn to decide or act.
words.easy: I've made my offer — [the ball is in your court].
ex: We've sent the contract, so [the ball is in their court].
I apologised; [the ball is in her court] now.
The union says [the ball is in the company's court].
col: the ball is in your court
put the ball in someone's court
words.nuance: Used when you've done your part and the next step belongs to the other person. The pronoun changes: in my / your / their court.
words.ety: From tennis: the ball is on your side, so you must hit it.

prec.s: I've told him I'm sorry and invited him for dinner. Now ___.
prec.ans: the ball is in his court
prec.why: The ball is in his court = it's his turn to act. A moot point no longer matters; touch and go means very uncertain; par for the course means normal and expected.

words.def: In agreement; sharing the same understanding.
words.simple: Agreeing and understanding things the same way.
words.easy: Before we start, let's make sure we're [on the same page].
ex: The two managers aren't [on the same page] about the budget.
We talked for an hour until everyone was [on the same page].
Good couples stay [on the same page] about money.
col: get everyone on the same page
words.nuance: On the same page is about shared understanding of a plan or goal. In the same boat is about sharing a difficult situation.
words.ety: Like readers all looking at the same page of a book.

prec.s: Before the client meeting, let's check that the whole team is ___ about the price.
prec.why: On the same page = in agreement and shared understanding. In the same boat means sharing a problem; on the fence means undecided; in hot water means in trouble.
